etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English curse, kors, cors, curs, from Old English cors, curs (“curse”), of unknown origin.

definitions.definition: A supernatural detriment or hindrance; a bane.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Malachi 2:2:
quote.text: If ye will not heare, and if yee will not lay it to heart, to giue glory vnto my name, saith the Lord of hostes; I will euen send a curse vpon you, and will curse your blessings: yea, I haue cursed them already, because yee doe not lay it to heart.

quote.citation: 1712 (date written), [Joseph] Addison, Cato, a Tragedy. […], London:  […]  J[acob] Tonson, […], published 1713, →OCLC, Act I, scene i, page 2:
quote.text: Oh Portius, is there not some choſen Curſe,Some hidden Thunder in the Stores of Heav’n,Red with uncommon Wrath, to blaſt the ManWho owes his Greatneſs to his Country’s Ruin?

definitions.definition: A prayer or imprecation that harm may befall someone.
The cause of great harm, evil, or misfortune; that which brings evil or severe affliction; torment.

quote.citation: c. 1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, The Famous Historie of Troylus and Cresseid. […] (First Quarto), London:  […]  G[eorge] Eld for R[ichard] Bonian and H[enry] Walley, […], published 1609, →OCLC, [Act II, scene iii]:
quote.text: The common curſe of mankinde, Folly and Ignorance […]

quote.citation: 2013 June 14, Sam Leith, “Where the profound meets the profane”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 189, number 1, page 37:
quote.text: Swearing doesn't just mean what we now understand by "dirty words". It is entwined, in social and linguistic history, with the other sort of swearing: vows and oaths. Consider for a moment the origins of almost any word we have for bad language – "profanity", "curses", "oaths" and "swearing" itself.

definitions.definition: (slang, dated, derogatory, usually with "the") A woman's menses.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English cursen, corsen, coursen, from Old English corsian, cursian (“to curse”), from the noun (see above).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To place a curse upon (a person or object).

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Numbers 22:10–12:
quote.text: And Balaam said unto God, Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, hath sent unto me, saying,Behold, there is a people come out of Egypt, which covereth the face of the earth: come now, curse me them; peradventure I shall be able to overcome them, and drive them out.And God said unto Balaam, Thou shalt not go with them; thou shalt not curse the people: for they are blessed.

quote.citation: 1910, Emerson Hough, “A Lady in Company”, in The Purchase Price: Or The Cause of Compromise, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Captain Edward Carlisle […] felt a curious sensation of helplessness seize upon him as he met her steady gaze, […] ; he could not tell what this prisoner might do. He cursed the fate which had assigned such a duty, cursed especially that fate which forced a gallant soldier to meet so superb a woman as this under handicap so hard.

definitions.definition: To call upon divine or supernatural power to send injury upon; to imprecate evil upon; to execrate.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Exodus 22:28, column 1:
quote.text: Thou ſhalt not […] curſe the ruler of thy people.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To speak or shout a vulgar curse or epithet.
(intransitive) To use offensive or morally inappropriate language.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Matthew 26:74, column 2:
quote.text: Then beganne hee to curſe and to ſweare […]

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii], page 9, column 1:
quote.text: […] his Spirits heare me, / And yet I needes muſt curſe.

definitions.definition: To bring great evil upon; to be the cause of serious harm or unhappiness to; to furnish with that which will be a cause of deep trouble; to afflict or injure grievously; to harass or torment.

quote.citation: 1712 May, [Alexander] Pope, transl., “The First Book of Statius his Thebais”, in Miscellaneous Poems and Translations. […], London:  […]  Bernard Lintott […], →OCLC, page 29:
quote.text: On Impious Realms, and barb’rous Kings, impoſe / Thy Plagues, and curſe 'em with ſuch Sons as thoſe.
